Mood Swings in Children
Mother seated on a couch leans toward young daughter

What are Mood Swings in Childhood?
Mood swings in childhood are rapidly shifting emotional states. A child may go from happy to sad to angry to exhausted in minutes. When mood swings are an issue, these shifts may occur every day or multiple times per day.

You may feel like your child’s anger is going from 0 to 60 in seconds. It might seem like the slightest thing goes wrong, and your child goes into orbit. One minute your child is silly and happy, and this mood can swing to excessively angry or sad in a short amount of time. 

“Your child may seem like one person one minute and someone entirely different the next. So you may catch yourself saying, ‘I wonder where my child went and how I can get him back?’ It’s like a moving roller coaster that you keep trying to get off of, or at least slow down.” 

It is normal for children or teens to have fluctuating moods sometimes. Throughout childhood, there are times when a kiddo’s moods may be in flux. However, there are certain kids for whom emotional regulation is extremely difficult. 

They may feel trapped in a prison of rapidly fluctuating moods. A pattern may emerge by which they feel amazing one day like they can conquer the world,

TOPIC:NURSEMAID’S ELBOW 

**DEFINITION:A pulled elbow is a result of the lower arm (radius bone) becoming partially dislocated (slipping out) of its normal position at the elbow joint. A pulled elbow is caused by a sudden pull on a child's lower arm or wrist, for example when a child is lifted up by one arm. It can also happen when a child falls.
**What causes nursemaid’s elbow?
Nursemaid’s elbow occurs when the ligament that holds your child’s radius in place at their elbow joint slips and the end of their radius shifts out of position, leading to their elbow becoming partially dislocated.
Even a little force can be enough to pull a young child’s elbow joint out of place. Common nursemaid elbow causes include:
**Swinging your child around by the hands or arms.
**Lifting your child up by the hands.
**Pulling your child’s arm through a jacket sleeve.
**Catching your child from falling by the hand.
**Pulling your child suddenly by the hand to avoid danger.
**What are the symptoms of nursemaid’s elbow?
*If you didn’t witness the injury, nursemaid’s elbow symptoms might not be obvious. Children will cry from the pain at first, but they might not complain much afterward. It won’t cause swelling. Pay attention if your child:
**Cries or expresses pain immediately after being pulled by the arms or hands.
**Has pain in their wrist and/or shoulder.
**Avoids moving or refuses to move their arm below their shoulder.
**Supports one arm with their other hand.
**Holds their arm straight or slightly bent and close to their body.
**Refuses to rotate their palm.
**DIAGNOSIS:Your child’s healthcare provider will perform a physical exam and ask about what happened at the time of injury. The physical exam will test your child’s range of motion and gently feel for tenderness at the elbow. Imaging tests aren’t required and often won’t show evidence of nursemaid elbow. However, an X-ray may rule out a fracture or break. 
**TREATMENT:pulled elbow in a child is usually treated by a doctor or nurse gently moving the arm to pop the bone back into place. This is called a reduction and can take only a few seconds. The child may cry briefly, but should feel better quickly and be able to use their arm again soon. 
**Here are some other things to know about treating a pulled elbow: 
**Pain relief
If there is discomfort, the doctor may recommend acetaminophen or ibuprofen. 
**Sling
**If the elbow can't be put back right away, or if the child needs more rest, the doctor may put a sling on the arm for 1–2 days.
**Return to normal
**Most children can use their arm normally within 20 minutes, but it may take longer.

6292.title: Collab topic
6292.body:
PULLED ELBOW 
*It is also known as nursemaid's elbow.
*It is a common injury in young children.
* It occurs when the radius bone in the forearm partially dislocates from the elbow joint.

*Causes:*

1. Sudden pulling or yanking of the arm.
2. Lifting or pulling the child by the hand.
3. Twisting or bending the arm.
4. Falling onto an outstretched hand.

*Symptoms:*

1. Pain or tenderness in the elbow.
2. Swelling or bruising.
3. Limited mobility or stiffness.
4. Child refuses to use the affected arm.
5. Visible deformity (in severe cases).

*Treatment:*

1. Reduction: Gentle manipulation to restore the radius bone to its normal position.
2. Immobilization: Temporary use of a splint or sling.
3. Pain management: Acetaminophen or ibuprofen.
4. Rest and ice.

*Prevention:*

1. Handle children's arms gently.
2. Avoid lifting or pulling by the hand.
3. Use proper lifting techniques.
4. Ensure children wear protective gear during sports.

*When to seek medical attention:*

1. Severe pain or swelling.
2. Difficulty moving the arm.
3. Visible deformity.
4. No improvement with treatment.
5. Recurring pulled elbows.

*Medical professional's assessment:*

1. Physical examination.
2. X-rays (to rule out fractures).
3. Orthopedic consultation (if necessary).

*Home care:*

1. Apply ice packs.
2. Elevate the affected arm.
3. Encourage rest.
4. Use pain medication (as directed).

Remember, if you suspect a pulled elbow, seek medical attention promptly to ensure proper treatment and prevent complications.

Dysphagia is a swallowing disorder that causes difficulty or pain while swallowing or attempting to swallow. Anyone can develop dysphagia, but it is more likely to occur in older people. This condition can make it difficult for people to get adequate nutrition and can significantly affect quality of life.

At Stanford, our gastrointestinal experts evaluate people who are having difficulty swallowing to determine the cause and plan symptom-relieving treatment. We target the root cause of swallowing problems and offer innovative treatment solutions to help you return to your best health.Dysphagia Types

Dysphagia has two main types: structural dysphagia, which results from changes to the actual structure of your esophagus, or dysphagia caused by esophageal motility (movement) issues. 

Structural dysphagia

In some cases, dysphagia results from certain changes to the physical structure of the esophagus. Commonly, dysphagia symptoms develop when areas of the esophagus become narrowed (strictures). Strictures form as a result of certain gastrointestinal conditions, like gastrointestinal reflux disease (GERD), or medical treatments like radiation therapy to the neck. 

Dysphagia related to esophageal motility

For some people, the symptoms of dysphagia result from problems with the esophagus’s ability to move food into the stomach. This dysfunction often results from damage to the nerves and muscles involved in the process of swallowing. However, certain medical conditions, like nervous system disorders, can affect the nerves involved in swallowing, causing dysphagia.

6294.title: Collab topic
6294.body:
Collab topic: Types of Dysphagia is prepared by Rizwana speech Therapist kurnool facility There are several types of dysphagia, classified based on the phase of swallowing affected, the underlying cause, or the nature of the swallowing difficulty. Here are some common types of dysphagia:

*Based on the Phase of Swallowing:*

1. *Oropharyngeal Dysphagia*: Difficulty with the oral and pharyngeal phases of swallowing, involving the mouth and throat.
2. *Pharyngeal Dysphagia*: Difficulty with the pharyngeal phase, involving the throat.
3. *Esophageal Dysphagia*: Difficulty with the esophageal phase, involving the esophagus.

*Based on the Underlying Cause:*

1. *Neurogenic Dysphagia*: Caused by neurological disorders, such as:
    - Stroke
    - Parkinson's disease
    - Multiple sclerosis
    - Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
    - Brain injury
2. *Structural Dysphagia*: Caused by physical obstructions, such as:
    - Head or neck cancer
    - Esophageal stricture
    - Achalasia
    - Zenker's diverticulum
3. *Functional Dysphagia*: No obvious physical cause, often related to:
    - Muscle weakness
    - Coordination problems
    - Sensory issues
4. *Psychogenic Dysphagia*: Caused by psychological factors, such as:
    - Anxiety
    - Depression
    - Eating disorders

*Based on the Nature of the Swallowing Difficulty:*

1. *Liquid Dysphagia*: Difficulty swallowing liquids.
2. *Solid Food Dysphagia*: Difficulty swallowing solid foods.
3. *Mixed Dysphagia*: Difficulty swallowing both liquids and solids.

*Other Types:*

1. *Transient Dysphagia*: Temporary swallowing difficulties, often resolving on their own.
2. *Chronic Dysphagia*: Long-term swallowing difficulties.
3. *Progressive Dysphagia*: Worsening swallowing difficulties over time.

*Pediatric-Specific Types:*

1. *Congenital Dysphagia*: Present at birth, often related to genetic conditions.
2. *Developmental Dysphagia*: Difficulty with swallowing development in children.

Accurate diagnosis and classification of dysphagia are crucial for effective treatment and management. A healthcare professional, such as a speech-language pathologist (SLP) or an otolaryngologist, typically conducts a comprehensive evaluation to determine the type and severity of dysphagia.

Swan neck deformity is a type of deformity that affects the finger, typically the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint. It is characterized by:

1. Hyperextension of the PIP joint (bending backward)
2. Flexion of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint (bending forward)

This creates a zigzag or swan-like appearance of the finger. Swan neck deformity can be caused by various factors, including:

1. Rheumatoid arthritis
2. Osteoarthritis
3. Trauma
4. Tendon imbalance
5. Neurological conditions (e.g., cerebral palsy, stroke)
6. Genetic conditions (e.g., Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)

Symptoms may include:

1. Pain
2. Limited mobility
3. Decreased grip strength
4. Aesthetic concerns

Treatment options vary depending on severity and underlying cause:

1. Splinting or orthotics
2. Physical therapy
3. Medications (e.g., pain relievers, anti-inflammatory)
4. Surgery (e.g., tendon reconstruction, joint replacement)

Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) affects memory in children in diverse ways, with some areas presenting challenges and others showing strengths.

### Memory Types Affected:
1. **Working Memory**: Children with autism may struggle with holding and manipulating information, affecting tasks like following instructions or problem-solving.
2. **Episodic Memory**: They often have difficulty recalling personal experiences or events in a detailed, emotional context.
3. **Semantic Memory**: This tends to be strong, allowing them to recall factual information easily.
4. **Procedural Memory**: Remembering how to do tasks, like riding a bike, is generally intact or even enhanced in some children.

### Memory Strengths:
- **Rote Memory**: Many children excel at memorizing facts, dates, or sequences.
- **Visual Memory**: They often have a strong ability to recall visual information, such as images or patterns.

### Memory Challenges:
- **Generalization**: Children may have trouble applying learned knowledge to new situations.
- **Social Memory**: Recalling social cues or interactions can be difficult, affecting relationships.
- **Prospective Memory**: Remembering to do things in the future, like bringing homework to school, may be a struggle.

### Impact on Learning:
- Memory issues can affect school performance, particularly in tasks requiring integration of new and old information.
- Visual aids, repetition, and structured routines are helpful strategies.

### Anxiety and Attention:
- High levels of anxiety or attention issues can further impair memory, especially if the child is not fully engaged in the information being presented.

In conclusion, memory in children with autism shows variability, with strengths in areas like visual or rote memory but challenges in generalizing information and recalling personal or social details. Understanding these patterns helps in providing targeted support.

6302.title: Collab Topic - Behavioural therapy
6302.body:
ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder) can affect individuals of all ages, but its impact can vary across different stages of life. Here's a breakdown of the challenges associated with ADHD at different ages:

*Childhood (6-12 years)*

- Difficulty following rules and completing homework
- Struggling to focus in class
- Impulsivity leads to social conflicts
- Hyperactivity disrupts playtime and daily routines
- Diagnosis often occurs during this stage

*Adolescence (13-19 years)*

- Increased academic demands exacerbate ADHD symptoms
- Social relationships become more complex, leading to struggles with friendships
- Emotional regulation difficulties lead to mood swings
- Risk-taking behaviors (e.g., substance abuse) increase
- Self-esteem and confidence may suffer

*Young Adulthood (20-30 years)*

- Transitioning to independent living can be overwhelming
- Time management and organization challenges persist
- Career and educational goals may be impacted
- Relationships and dating can be difficult
- Substance abuse and addiction risks remain

*Adulthood (31-50 years)*

- Work-life balance and stress management become critical
- ADHD symptoms may affect job performance and career advancement
- Relationships with family and friends can be strained
- Health concerns (e.g., sleep disorders, anxiety) may arise
- Self-awareness and coping strategies become essential

*Middle Age (51+ years)*

- ADHD symptoms may decrease, but executive function deficits remain
- Health concerns (e.g., cognitive decline, chronic illnesses) increase
- Retirement planning and transitions can be challenging
- Social isolation and loneliness may become issues
- Reflection on life accomplishments and regrets may occur

While ADHD symptoms may change over time, their impact can be significant at any age. It's essential to recognize the challenges and adapt coping strategies to manage ADHD effectively.

*Key Takeaways:*

1. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial.
2. Develop coping strategies and self-awareness.
3. Build a support network (family, friends, professionals).
4. Stay organized and manage time effectively.
5. Prioritize physical and mental well-being.

Keep in mind that every individual's experience with ADHD is unique, and the level of difficulty can vary greatly. Consult with a healthcare professional for personalized guidance and support.

Is having ADHD is a learning disability 
Here’s a simple explanation in points:

1. **ADHD is not a learning disability** – ADHD affects attention, focus, and self-control, but it is different from a learning disability.
   
2. **It can still impact learning** – Kids with ADHD may struggle to focus, stay organized, or complete tasks, making learning harder.

4. **Some kids have both** – It’s possible for a child to have ADHD and a learning disability at the same time.

5. **Support helps** – With the right help (extra time, strategies, or special support), kids with ADHD can still do well in school.

Borderline Intellectual Functioning (BIF) is typically defined as having an IQ score between 71 and 84, which is below the average range but not severe enough to be classified as intellectual disability.

Here's a breakdown of IQ levels and their corresponding classifications:

*IQ Classification*

- Average: 85-114
- Below Average: 70-84 (Borderline Intellectual Functioning)
- Intellectual Disability:
    - Mild: 50-69
    - Moderate: 35-49
    - Severe: 20-34
    - Profound: Below 20

*Borderline Intellectual Functioning Characteristics*

- Difficulty with:
    - Abstract thinking
    - Problem-solving
    - Learning new skills
    - Adaptive behavior
- May need support in:
    - Daily living tasks
    - Social interactions
    - Vocational training
- May experience:
    - Academic struggles
    - Social isolation
    - Emotional difficulties

*Assessment and Diagnosis*

- IQ tests (e.g., Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, WAIS)
- Adaptive behavior assessments (e.g., Adaptive Behavior Assessment System, ABAS)
- Clinical evaluation and observation
- Medical and psychological history

*Important Notes*

- IQ scores are not the sole determining factor for BIF.
- Cultural, environmental, and socioeconomic factors can influence IQ scores.
- BIF is not a formal diagnosis in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5).
- Support and accommodations can help individuals with BIF lead fulfilling lives.

Keep in mind that IQ scores and classifications are not always precise and should be considered in conjunction with other factors.

The main difference between articulation and phonological disorders is that articulation disorders affect the production of individual sounds, while phonological disorders affect more than one sound

Articulation disorders:

These disorders affect the motor functions required to make certain speech sounds. Symptoms include mispronouncing words, difficulty saying syllables, and leaving out or adding sounds. For example, a child with an articulation disorder might not be able to form the sound "th" and always use "f" instead.

Phonological disorders:

These disorders affect the ability to put sounds together correctly. Symptoms include using incorrect speech patterns, such as dropping the first or last sound of a word or replacing certain sounds for others. For example, a child with a phonological disorder might be able to make the sound "d" on its own, but when they try to say a word that starts with "d," they might swap it out with a "g".

DOWN SYNDROME
*Down syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.

*Causes and Risk Factors:*

1. Genetic mutation: Extra copy of chromosome 21.
2. Advanced maternal age (35+ years).
3. Family history.
4. Genetic carriers.

*Symptoms:*

1. Intellectual disability.
2. Delayed speech and language development.
3. Physical characteristics:
    - Flat face.
    - Short neck.
    - Protruding tongue.
    - Small ears.
    - Short stature.
4. Health issues:
    - Congenital heart defects.
    - Vision and hearing problems.
    - Respiratory issues.
    - Increased risk of Alzheimer's.

*Diagnosis:*

1. Prenatal testing (amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling).
2. Postnatal diagnosis (physical examination, genetic testing).

*Treatment and Management:*

1. Early intervention programs.
2. Speech and language therapy.
3. Occupational and physical therapy.
4. Medications for related health issues.
5. Supportive care.

*Types of Down Syndrome:*

1. Trisomy 21 (most common).
2. Mosaicism (mix of normal and abnormal cells).
3. Translocation (part of chromosome 21 attached to another chromosome).

*Interesting Facts:*

1. 1 in 700 births.
2. Over 5 million people worldwide have Down syndrome.
3. Life expectancy: 50-60 years (increasing with medical advancements).
4. Individuals with Down syndrome can lead fulfilling lives with proper support.

There are a number of measures that can help reduce speech errors in children with autism, including:

Communication training
Teaches basic speech and language skills, such as phrases and single words. 
Motor planning and sequencing
Helps children practice the movement patterns needed for speech. 
Repetitive practice
Helps children learn to produce sounds and words more consistently and automatically. 
Visual and auditory cues
Helps children see and hear their own production, making it easier to make adjustments. 
Multi-sensory approaches
Uses touch cues on the face to guide movements, or gestures to support speech sound development. 
Within-stimulus prompts
Uses exaggerated presentation of a part of the model to troubleshoot incorrectly articulated sounds. 
Extra-stimulus prompts
Uses techniques such as holding the child's jaw slightly open, prompting the tongue position, or touching the cheeks. 
Occupational therapy
Helps individuals with autism improve their ability to participate in daily activities and promote self-regulation. 
Some children with autism may never develop oral speech and language skills. For these children, the goal may be to learn to communicate using gestures or a symbol system.

6314.body:
Ataxic gait is a type of abnormal gait characterized by a lack of coordination and balance. It is often associated with damage to the cerebellum, which is the part of the brain responsible for coordinating movements.

Characteristics of Ataxic Gait:
1. *Wide-based gait*: People with ataxic gait often walk with their feet far apart to compensate for their lack of balance.
2. *Unsteady and staggering*: Ataxic gait is characterized by an unsteady and staggering walk, with a tendency to veer from side to side.
3. *Difficulty with balance*: Individuals with ataxic gait often have trouble maintaining their balance, especially when standing on one foot or walking on uneven surfaces.
4. *Tremors and dysmetria*: Ataxic gait can also be accompanied by tremors (shaking movements) and dysmetria (difficulty judging distances and spatial relationships).

Causes of Ataxic Gait:
1. *Cerebellar damage*: Damage to the cerebellum, such as from a stroke, traumatic brain injury, or neurodegenerative disease, can cause ataxic gait.
2. *Neurodegenerative diseases*: Conditions such as multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and Friedreich's ataxia can cause ataxic gait.
3. *Vitamin deficiencies*: Deficiencies in vitamins such as vitamin B12 can cause ataxic gait.
4. *Medications*: Certain medications, such as sedatives and anticonvulsants, can cause ataxic gait as a side effect.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
1. *Physical examination*: A physical examination by a healthcare professional can help diagnose ataxic gait.
2. *Imaging tests*: Imaging tests such as MRI or CT scans may be ordered to rule out underlying conditions that may be causing the ataxic gait.
3. *Physical therapy*: Physical therapy can help improve balance, coordination, and gait.
4. *Medications*: Medications may be prescribed to manage underlying conditions that are contributing to the ataxic gait.

TOPIC:KNOCK KNEES 
Knock knees, also known as genu varum, is a condition where the knees touch or nearly touch each other, while the ankles remain apart. Here's an overview:
Causes
1. *Genetics*: Family history can play a role.
2. *Growth and development*: Normal variation in childhood growth patterns.
3. *Abnormal bone growth*: Conditions like rickets or osteomalacia.
4. *Injury or trauma*: Fractures or injuries affecting the knee or leg.
5. *Neurological conditions*: Cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, or other conditions affecting muscle tone.
Symptoms
1. *Visible knee deformity*: Knees touch or nearly touch.
2. *Uneven gait*: Abnormal walking pattern.
3. *Pain*: Knee pain or discomfort, especially after activity.
4. *Instability*: Difficulty standing or walking.
Diagnosis
1. *Physical examination*: Orthopedic evaluation.
2. *Imaging tests*: X-rays, CT scans, or MRI to assess bone growth and alignment.
Treatment
1. *Observation*: Monitoring growth and development.
2. *Orthotics*: Bracing or shoe inserts to support knee alignment.
3. *Physical therapy*: Strengthening exercises for surrounding muscles.
4. *Surgery*: In severe cases, osteotomy or other surgical procedures may be necessary.
Complications
1. *Osteoarthritis*: Increased risk of knee arthritis.
2. *Gait abnormalities*: Persistent uneven gait.
3. *Self-esteem issues*: Potential impact on self-confidence.
Prevention
1. *Maintain a healthy weight*: Reduce pressure on knees.
2. *Exercise regularly*: Strengthen surrounding muscles.
3. *Wear proper footwear*: Supportive shoes with good arch support.

By Chaitanya Garu  (SE) 
Learning disabilities are neurologically based processing difficulties that can affect an individual's ability to learn and perform academic tasks. Here are different types of learning disabilities:
1. Dyslexia
- Difficulty reading, decoding, and spelling words
- Trouble with phonemic awareness, fluency, and comprehension
- May struggle with writing, organization, and time management
2. Dysgraphia
- Difficulty writing, typing, and composing written language

3. Dyscalculia
- Difficulty understanding and working with numbers
- Trouble with math concepts, problem-solving, and calculations
- May struggle with time, money, and measurement concepts
4. Dyspraxia
- Difficulty with motor skills, coordination, and planning
- Trouble with balance, posture, and movement
- May struggle with handwriting, using scissors, and other fine motor tasks
5. Auditory Processing Disorder (APD)
- Difficulty processing and understanding auditory information
- Trouble with listening, following directions, and distinguishing sounds
- May struggle with reading, writing, and speaking
6. Visual Processing Disorder (VPD)
- Difficulty processing and understanding visual information
- Trouble with reading, writing, and math
- May struggle with recognizing shapes, sizes, and colors
7. Language-Based Learning Disabilities
- Difficulty with language skills, such as reading, writing, and speaking
- Trouble with vocabulary, grammar, and comprehension
- May struggle with social interactions and communication
8. Nonverbal Learning Disabilities (NVLD)
- Difficulty with nonverbal skills, such as spatial relationships and visual-spatial skills

Proprioception is the ability to sense the position, orientation, and movement of your body. It's crucial for balance, posture, and coordinated movements. Here's a breakdown:

Types of Proprioception
1. *Static proprioception*: Sensing body position and orientation in space.
2. *Dynamic proprioception*: Sensing movement and changes in body position.

Proprioceptors
Specialized sensors called proprioceptors detect changes in muscle length, tension, and joint angle. They're found in:

1. Muscles
2. Tendons
3. Joints
4. Ligaments

Functions of Proprioception
1. *Balance and posture*: Maintaining upright posture and balance.
2. *Movement coordination*: Guiding voluntary movements, like walking or grasping.
3. *Muscle tone regulation*: Adjusting muscle tension to maintain posture and movement.

Impaired Proprioception
Can result from:

1. Neurological conditions (e.g., stroke, Parkinson's disease)
2. Musculoskeletal injuries (e.g., sprains, strains)
3. Sensory deficits (e.g., numbness, tingling)

Exercises to Improve Proprioception
1. *Balance exercises*: Single-leg stance, balance boards, or BOSU ball training.
2. *Proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF)*: Techniques that stimulate proprioceptors.
3. *Yoga and tai chi*: Exercises that focus on body awareness and movement control.

6320.body:
Torticollis, also known as wry neck, is a condition characterized by an abnormal tilt or rotation of the head and neck. Here's an overview:

Types of Torticollis
1. *Congenital torticollis*: Present at birth, often due to intrauterine positioning or birth trauma.
2. *Acquired torticollis*: Develops later in life, often due to injury, infection, or neurological conditions.
3. *Spasmodic torticollis*: A type of dystonia, characterized by involuntary muscle contractions.

Causes
1. *Muscle imbalance*: Weakness or tightness in the neck muscles.
2. *Bone or joint abnormalities*: Misalignment or deformities in the cervical spine.
3. *Neurological conditions*: Stroke, cerebral palsy, or other conditions affecting the brain and nervous system.
4. *Injury or trauma*: Whiplash, falls, or other injuries.

Symptoms
1. *Abnormal head position*: Tilted or rotated head and neck.
2. *Limited range of motion*: Difficulty moving the head or neck.
3. *Pain or discomfort*: Neck pain, stiffness, or muscle spasms.
4. *Difficulty with daily activities*: Trouble with feeding, sleeping, or other daily tasks.

Diagnosis
1. *Physical examination*: Evaluation of head and neck position, range of motion, and muscle tone.
2. *Imaging studies*: X-rays, CT scans, or MRI to rule out underlying bone or joint abnormalities.
3. *Neurological examination*: Assessment of neurological function, including reflexes and muscle strength.

Treatment
1. *Physical therapy*: Stretching, strengthening, and range-of-motion exercises.
2. *Occupational therapy*: Adaptation of daily activities and environments.
3. *Botulinum toxin injections*: To relax muscle spasms.
4. *Surgery*: In some cases, to correct underlying bone or joint abnormalities.

Complications
1. *Chronic pain*: Persistent neck pain or discomfort.
2. *Limited mobility*: Permanent limitation in range of motion.
3. *Neurological problems*: In rare cases, torticollis can lead to neurological complications, such as nerve damage or spinal cord injury.

6321.title: Collab topic - Occupational Therapy
6321.body:
A pulled elbow, also known as nursemaid's elbow, is a common injury that occurs when the radial head subluxates (partially dislocates) from the annular ligament. It typically affects children under the age of 5.

Causes:

- Sudden pulling or yanking of the child's arm, often while holding hands or lifting.
- Twisting or turning of the arm.
- Falling onto an outstretched hand.

Symptoms:

- Sudden onset of pain and crying.
- Refusal to move the affected arm.
- Holding the arm still and close to the body.
- Swelling or bruising may be present, but not always.

Treatment:

- Reduction: A healthcare professional will perform a gentle maneuver to guide the radial head back into place.
- Immobilization: The arm may be immobilized in a sling or cast to allow the annular ligament to heal.
- Pain management: Acetaminophen or ibuprofen may be prescribed to manage pain and discomfort.
- Follow-up: A follow-up appointment with a healthcare professional is necessary to ensure the elbow has fully recovered.

Prevention:

- Avoid pulling or yanking the child's arm.
- Lift the child carefully, avoiding twisting or turning motions.
- Supervise the child during play to prevent falls.
- Teach the child how to fall safely, with arms curled in and head protected.

Froala Editor

6322.title: Collab topic - Occupational Therapy
6322.body:
Cubital valgus, also known as gunstock deformity, is a condition where the elbow joint is angled outward, resulting in a deformity of the arm. Here's an overview:
Causes
1. *Fractures*: Fractures of the elbow, particularly those involving the lateral condyle, can lead to cubital valgus.
2. *Growth disturbances*: Growth disturbances, such as nonunion or malunion of the lateral condyle, can cause cubital valgus.
3. *Neurological conditions*: Neurological conditions, such as cerebral palsy or muscular dystrophy, can lead to muscle imbalances that cause cubital valgus.
Symptoms
1. *Elbow deformity*: The elbow joint is angled outward, resulting in a visible deformity.
2. *Limited mobility*: Limited range of motion in the elbow joint.
Diagnosis
1. *Physical examination*: A doctor will examine the elbow joint and assess range of motion, strength, and deformity.
2. *Imaging studies*: X-rays, CT scans, or MRI scans may be ordered to evaluate the elbow joint and surrounding tissues.
Treatment
1. *Observation*: Mild cases may be monitored with regular follow-up appointments.
2. *Physical therapy*: Physical therapy can help improve range of motion, strength, and function.
Complications
1. *Chronic pain*: Untreated cubital valgus can lead to chronic pain and discomfort.
2. *Limited mobility*: Untreated cubital valgus can result in permanent limited mobility.

6326.title: Collab Topic Occupational therapy
6326.body:
Torticollis is a condition where your baby’s neck muscles cause their head to twist and tilt to one side. It may look like your infant’s neck is rotated at an odd angle. The top of their head may be tilted to one side and their chin may be tilted to the other side.Torticollis is also called wryneck. Torticollis comes from the Latin words “tortus,” which means twisted, and “collum,” which means neck. Torticollis is fairly common in babies and children. Torticollis may be present at birth (congenital). Or it may develop later in infancy or childhood (acquired).
Symptoms and Causes:
Short, tight sternocleidomastoid muscles (SCMs) can cause torticollis, a condition in which your baby’s head twists and tilts to one side.
Short, tight sternocleidomastoid muscles can cause torticollis.
Torticollis is a condition where your baby’s neck muscles cause their head to twist and tilt to one side. It may look like your infant’s neck is rotated at an odd angle. The top of their head may be tilted to one side and their chin may be tilted to the other side.
Torticollis is also called wryneck. Torticollis comes from the Latin words “tortus,” which means twisted, and “collum,” which means neck. Torticollis is fairly common in babies and children. Torticollis may be present at birth (congenital). Or it may develop later in infancy or childhood (acquired).
Congenital torticollis is the most common type of torticollis. It’s usually painless to your infant. You may not notice it until your baby is a few weeks old. Once they start to gain more control of their head, you may spot it.
Acquired torticollis usually occurs in the first four to six months of your baby’s life or later. You may notice it suddenly or it may come on more slowly. Acquired torticollis may be harmless (benign) or it may be a sign of a more serious health issue.
Symptoms and Causes
What are the symptoms of torticollis?
Symptoms of congenital torticollis may include:
Your baby’s head tilts to one side and chin tilts to the other side.
Limited movement of your baby’s head and neck.
One of your baby’s shoulders is higher than the other.
Neck muscle tightness or stiffness.
Swollen neck muscles.
Small pea-sized lump in one of your baby’s neck muscles.
Most often, stretching exercises and position changes can treat congenital torticollis. Your baby’s healthcare provider will teach you how to stretch your baby’s neck muscles. You’ll need to gently move your baby’s head to the opposite side. You’ll want to practice torticollis stretches several times a day. Over time, slowly increase the movements.
For position changes, lay your baby on their back with their head positioned to the opposite side during naps and at bedtime. When your baby’s awake, move toys and other objects so they have to practice turning their neck in the opposite direction
